campaign.executiveSummary: The OWASP Juice Shop v20.0.0 instance at http://127.0.0.1:3000 exhibits critical security vulnerabilities across multiple domains. SQL injection in the login and product search endpoints enables complete authentication bypass and full database exfiltration including all user credentials, TOTP secrets, and security answers. Mass assignment on user registration allows arbitrary admin account creation. JWT algorithm confusion (alg:none) permits forging authentication tokens for any user. DOM XSS in the search functionality chains to session hijacking. Additional high-severity findings include XXE processing, IDOR-based cross-user data access, unauthenticated product tampering, and null byte injection bypassing file access restrictions.

findings.title: SQL Injection Authentication Bypass - Admin Login
findings.description: The login endpoint at /rest/user/login is vulnerable to SQL injection in the email parameter. By injecting `' OR 1=1--` in the email field, the application authenticates as the first user in the database (admin@juice-sh.op) with role 'admin', bypassing all authentication controls. A valid JWT token with admin privileges is returned.
findings.remediation: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) for all SQL operations. Never concatenate user input into SQL strings. Implement an ORM with proper input binding.

findings.title: UNION-based SQL Injection - Product Search (Full Database Exfiltration)
findings.description: The product search endpoint /rest/products/search is vulnerable to UNION-based SQL injection. By injecting UNION SELECT statements through the q parameter, an attacker can extract the complete database schema (sqlite_master), all user emails and password hashes from the Users table, security answers, card numbers, and any other data from the SQLite database. 23 user credential pairs (email:password_hash) were extracted.
findings.remediation: Use parameterized queries for search functionality. Implement input validation and sanitization for the search parameter. Apply the principle of least privilege to database accounts.

findings.title: Confidential Document Exposure - FTP Directory Listing
findings.description: The /ftp/ directory is publicly accessible and lists multiple sensitive files including acquisitions.md (marked confidential, contains acquisition plans), coupons_2013.md.bak (backup coupon data), package.json.bak and package-lock.json.bak (application dependencies with potential version info), incident-support.kdbx (KeePass password database), encrypt.pyc (Python encryption code), and suspicious_errors.yml. Despite robots.txt disallowing /ftp, the files are directly accessible.
findings.remediation: Remove the /ftp/ directory from public access. Implement proper access controls. Remove sensitive files from the web server. Move backup files to secure storage.

findings.title: Null Byte Injection - FTP File Extension Bypass
findings.description: The FTP file server at /ftp/ restricts downloads to .md and .pdf files. However, appending a URL-encoded null byte (%2500) followed by .md to any filename bypasses the extension validation. This allows downloading any file from the FTP directory regardless of its actual extension, including .bak backup files, .gg files, .yml configuration files, and .kdbx password databases.
findings.remediation: Fix the file extension validation to properly handle null bytes. Implement a whitelist approach for allowed files rather than extension-based filtering. Strip null bytes from request paths before processing.

findings.title: SQL Injection - Security Answers Extraction via UNION SELECT
findings.description: Using the UNION-based SQL injection in /rest/products/search, all security question answers for every user were extracted from the SecurityAnswers table. These answers (though hashed) are linked by UserId and SecurityQuestionId, enabling password reset attacks. Combined with the user credentials dump, this constitutes a complete compromise of all user account recovery mechanisms.
findings.remediation: Use parameterized queries. Implement proper input validation. Hash security answers with unique salts per user.

findings.title: Exposed Prometheus Metrics Endpoint
findings.description: The /metrics endpoint exposes Prometheus metrics without authentication, revealing internal application metrics including HTTP request counts by status code, file upload errors, LLM token usage, startup duration, and custom juiceshop-prefixed metrics. This information can be used by attackers to understand application behavior and identify attack patterns.
findings.remediation: Restrict access to /metrics endpoint with authentication or limit it to internal network access only.

findings.title: Wallet Mnemonic Phrase Exposure in Public Feedback
findings.description: A cryptocurrency wallet mnemonic phrase is exposed in public feedback from UserId 21: 'purpose betray marriage blame crunch monitor spin slide donate sport lift clutch'. This is a 12-word BIP-39 mnemonic that could be used to reconstruct the wallet and steal any funds. The feedback is accessible without authentication at /api/Feedbacks/.
findings.remediation: Implement content filtering on user-submitted feedback to redact sensitive data. Apply input validation to prevent posting of credential-like patterns.

findings.title: Exposed JWT RSA Public Key - Algorithm Confusion Attack Vector
findings.description: The JWT RSA public key is exposed at /encryptionkeys/jwt.pub. This key can be used in an RS256-to-HS256 algorithm confusion attack where the attacker signs a JWT using the public key as an HMAC secret. If the server accepts both RS256 and HS256 algorithms, an attacker could forge arbitrary JWTs to impersonate any user. The /encryptionkeys/ directory also exposes premium.key containing the value '1337133713371337.EA99A61D92D2955B1E9285B55BF2AD42'.
findings.remediation: Remove the /encryptionkeys/ directory from public access. Store cryptographic keys securely and never expose them through the web server. Validate the JWT algorithm server-side to prevent algorithm confusion attacks.

findings.title: Business Logic Flaw - Zero Star Rating Accepted
findings.description: The Feedbacks API accepts a rating of 0, bypassing the expected minimum rating of 1 star. While the Angular client-side validation enforces a minimum of 1 star, the API endpoint can be called directly with rating:0, allowing submission of zero-star ratings that should not be possible.
findings.remediation: Implement server-side validation to enforce minimum rating of 1 star on the Feedbacks API endpoint.

findings.title: CAPTCHA Answer Leaked in REST API Response
findings.description: The CAPTCHA REST API at /rest/captcha/ returns both the captcha challenge and its answer in the same response. This completely defeats the purpose of the CAPTCHA, as an attacker can programmatically read the answer and submit forms automatically. The response includes captchaId, captcha (the math expression), and answer (the solution).
findings.remediation: Never include the captcha answer in the API response. Store the answer server-side only, keyed by captchaId, and validate it on submission without exposing it.

findings.title: Product Tampering - Unauthenticated Price/Description Modification
findings.description: The PUT /api/Products/{id} endpoint allows unauthenticated modification of product data, including price and description. An attacker can change any product's price to an arbitrary value (e.g., 0.01) without authentication. The product Apple Juice (1000ml) was successfully modified with price changed to 0.01. The description was sanitized (iframe tag was stripped), but the price change persisted, demonstrating a complete lack of authorization controls on product modification.
findings.remediation: Implement proper authentication and authorization checks on all product modification endpoints. Only admin users should be able to modify product data. Validate price ranges server-side.

findings.title: IDOR - Cross-User Basket Access
findings.description: The /rest/basket/{id} endpoint allows authenticated users to access any user's basket by simply changing the basket ID. Using admin's JWT token (user ID 1), baskets belonging to user ID 2 (basket 2) and user ID 3 (basket 3) were successfully accessed. No ownership validation is performed — any authenticated user can view and potentially modify any other user's shopping basket, exposing product preferences and enabling basket manipulation attacks.
findings.remediation: Implement server-side ownership validation. Verify that the authenticated user's ID matches the basket's UserId before returning data. Use user-scoped queries instead of direct ID lookups.

findings.title: Targeted SQL Injection - Login as Specific User
findings.description: The SQL injection on /rest/user/login can be used to log in as any specific user by crafting the email payload with the target user's email followed by ' AND 1=1--. For example, using email 'bender@juice-sh.op' AND 1=1--' successfully authenticates as bender@juice-sh.op without knowing their password. This was confirmed by receiving a valid JWT token with bender's identity.
findings.remediation: Use parameterized queries for all authentication operations. Implement prepared statements. Add rate limiting and account lockout mechanisms.

findings.title: Forged Product Review - Cross-User Review Modification (IDOR)
findings.description: The PATCH /rest/products/reviews endpoint allows any authenticated user to modify any other user's product review by specifying the review _id (MongoDB ObjectId). Using admin's JWT token, a review authored by jim@juice-sh.op (MongoDB _id: BgP4myoipyS5pnyke) was successfully modified to change its message. The original message was replaced with 'Forged review by admin'. No ownership validation is performed on review modification.
findings.remediation: Implement ownership validation on review modification. Verify that the authenticated user's email matches the review's author before allowing modification.

findings.title: Exposed Access Logs - Server Request History Disclosure
findings.description: The /support/logs/ directory is publicly accessible and contains server access log files including access.log.2026-07-27, access.log.2026-07-28, and audit.json. The access logs contain complete HTTP request history with IP addresses, timestamps, request paths (including SQL injection payloads), response codes, and user agents. This exposes the server's entire request history to any visitor.
findings.remediation: Restrict access to the /support/logs/ directory. Implement authentication for log access. Move log files to a secure location not served by the web server.

findings.title: TOTP Secret Extraction via SQL Injection - 2FA Bypass
findings.description: Using UNION-based SQL injection on the product search, the TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) secret for user ID 10 (wurstbrot@juice-sh.op) was extracted: IFTXE3SPOEYVURT2MRYGI52TKJ4HC3KH. This TOTP secret can be used to generate valid 2FA codes, completely bypassing the two-factor authentication protection for this account. All other users have empty totpSecret fields.
findings.remediation: Fix the SQL injection vulnerability. Encrypt TOTP secrets at rest. Never store TOTP secrets in plaintext in the database.

findings.title: Verbose Stack Trace Disclosure in Error Responses
findings.description: Multiple error responses across the application expose verbose stack traces including full file paths (/juice-shop/build/routes/fileServer.js, /juice-shop/build/routes/login.js, /juice-shop/build/lib/insecurity.js), framework versions (Express ^4.22.1), internal module paths (sequelize, morgan, node_modules), and function names. These stack traces help attackers understand the application's internal structure and identify specific attack vectors.
findings.remediation: Disable verbose error messages in production. Implement a custom error handler that returns generic error messages. Log detailed errors server-side only.

findings.title: Forged Feedback - User ID Spoofing in Feedback Submission
findings.description: The Feedback API at POST /api/Feedbacks/ accepts a UserId field in the request body without validation. An unauthenticated user can submit feedback attributed to any user by specifying their UserId. This was demonstrated by submitting feedback with UserId:2 without any authentication token, successfully creating feedback (id:10) attributed to user 2.
findings.remediation: Derive the UserId from the authenticated session/JWT token rather than from the request body. Never trust client-supplied user identifiers for data association.

findings.title: XXE Entity Processing in B2B Order XML Endpoint
findings.description: The B2B order endpoint at POST /b2b/v2/orders accepts XML input and processes XML external entities (XXE). When sending a DOCTYPE definition with an entity referencing file:///etc/passwd, the server processes the DTD without error and creates the order. The entity resolution is blind (the resolved content is not reflected in the response), but the successful order creation confirms the XML parser processes external entities. This can be leveraged for server-side file reading, SSRF, or data exfiltration via out-of-band channels.
findings.remediation: Disable DTD processing and external entity resolution in the XML parser. Use JSON for B2B orders instead of XML. If XML is required, use a properly configured parser that blocks XXE.

findings.title: Soft-Deleted Products Accessible via SQL Injection (Christmas Special)
findings.description: Using the UNION-based SQL injection, 10 soft-deleted products were discovered including 'Christmas Super-Surprise-Box (2014 Edition)' (id:10), 'Rippertuer Special Juice' (id:11), and '20th Anniversary Celebration Ticket' (id:44). These products have deletedAt timestamps set and are not visible through normal product listings. The SQL injection bypasses the soft-delete filter, exposing hidden/discontinued product data.
findings.remediation: Fix the SQL injection vulnerability. Implement proper access controls for soft-deleted records.

findings.title: User Enumeration via Security Question Endpoint
findings.description: The /rest/user/security-question endpoint accepts an email parameter and returns the user's security question without authentication. This can be used to enumerate valid email addresses (different responses for existing vs non-existing users) and to gather information needed for password reset attacks. For example, jim@juice-sh.op uses question 'Your eldest siblings middle name?' (question id 1).
findings.remediation: Rate limit the security question endpoint. Consider not revealing which security question a user has chosen until after additional verification.

findings.title: Mass Assignment - Admin Role via User Registration
findings.description: The user registration endpoint at POST /api/Users/ accepts a 'role' field in the request body, allowing any unauthenticated user to register a new account with admin privileges. A test account (id:24, email:test@test.com) was successfully created with role 'admin' by including "role":"admin" in the registration request. This is a mass assignment / over-privileged registration vulnerability that allows immediate privilege escalation without any existing account.
findings.remediation: Implement a whitelist of allowed fields for user registration. Never accept role, isActive, or other security-sensitive fields from client requests. Use a DTO pattern to strip unauthorized fields before processing.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Admin Configuration Disclosure
findings.description: The /rest/admin/application-configuration endpoint is accessible without any authentication and returns the complete application configuration including server settings (port, baseUrl), Google OAuth client ID, social media URLs, chatbot configuration (LLM model: gemma4:e4b), security.txt details, promotion video paths, encryption key locations, and authorized redirect URIs. This provides attackers with a comprehensive blueprint of the application's infrastructure and security settings.
findings.remediation: Restrict access to admin configuration endpoints. Require authentication and admin role to access /rest/admin/* endpoints.

findings.title: Sensitive Data Exposure - Premium Content Decryption Key
findings.description: The /encryptionkeys/premium.key file is publicly accessible and contains the premium content decryption key: '1337133713371337.EA99A61D92D2955B1E9285B55BF2AD42'. This key can be used to decrypt premium/paid content, bypassing the premium paywall. The key appears to be a combination of a repeated pattern and an MD5-like hash.
findings.remediation: Remove the /encryptionkeys/ directory from public access. Store encryption keys securely server-side only.

findings.title: Exposed Coupon Codes in Backup File (via Null Byte Bypass)
findings.description: The file coupons_2013.md.bak was accessed via the null byte bypass (%2500.md) and contains 12 encoded coupon codes from 2013. These codes follow a consistent pattern (ending with gC7sn or gC7ss) and could potentially be decoded or used to understand the coupon generation algorithm for creating valid current coupons.
findings.remediation: Remove backup files from the web server. Fix the null byte injection vulnerability. Implement proper file access controls.

findings.title: DOM XSS via Search Query Parameter - iframe src=javascript
findings.description: The OWASP Juice Shop search functionality is vulnerable to DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting (XSS). The search query parameter `q` in the URL hash fragment (/#/search?q=) is reflected into the DOM without proper sanitization. An iframe element with a javascript: URI in its src attribute triggers JavaScript execution when rendered. The payload `<iframe src="javascript:alert('xss')">` successfully triggers an alert() dialog, confirming arbitrary JavaScript execution in the context of the application. This can be exploited for session hijacking, cookie theft, or arbitrary actions on behalf of the victim user.

findings.title: DOM XSS via Search Query Parameter - img onerror
findings.description: A second DOM XSS vector was confirmed in the search functionality using an img tag with an onerror event handler. The payload `<img src=x onerror=alert("xss2")>` is rendered into the DOM unsanitized, and because the src attribute points to a non-existent resource, the onerror handler fires, executing arbitrary JavaScript. The alert was triggered twice (likely due to Angular change detection re-rendering), proving the payload executes reliably. This can be weaponized to steal session tokens, perform actions on behalf of the user, or redirect to phishing pages.

findings.title: JWT Token Stores Sensitive Data Including Password Hash
findings.description: The JWT token issued upon authentication contains the complete user record including the MD5 password hash (0192023a7bbd73250516f069df18b500), email, role, profile image path, TOTP secret field, creation timestamps, and other sensitive fields. This data is exposed to any client-side JavaScript since the token is stored in localStorage and as a non-httpOnly cookie. An attacker who obtains this token (e.g., via XSS) can extract the password hash and attempt offline cracking. The password hash is MD5 (unsalted), making it trivially crackable.

findings.title: JWT Token Cookie Missing HttpOnly and Secure Flags
findings.description: The authentication token is stored in a cookie named 'token' without HttpOnly or Secure flags. This means the token is accessible via JavaScript (document.cookie) and can be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections. Combined with the confirmed DOM XSS vulnerability, an attacker can steal the authentication token via a crafted XSS payload. The cookie also lacks the SameSite=Strict attribute (set to Lax), providing only partial CSRF protection.

findings.title: CAPTCHA Answer Leaked in REST API Response Enabling Automated Bypass
findings.description: The REST API endpoint /rest/captcha/ returns the CAPTCHA answer alongside the CAPTCHA challenge in the JSON response. The response includes captchaId, captcha expression (e.g., '4*10+9'), and the answer field (e.g., '49'). This completely defeats the purpose of the CAPTCHA, allowing automated systems to solve it by simply reading the response. This was exploited to submit automated feedback via the /api/Feedbacks/ endpoint, bypassing the CAPTCHA protection entirely.

findings.title: Client-Side Validation Bypass - Zero-Star and Negative Rating Accepted
findings.description: The feedback form enforces a minimum rating of 1 star on the client side, but the server-side API accepts any numeric value including 0 and negative numbers. By sending a direct POST request to /api/Feedbacks/ with rating=0 or rating=-1, the server accepts and stores the feedback with HTTP 201. This bypasses the client-side validation constraint and allows submission of invalid business data. The UI prevents selecting zero stars, but the API has no server-side validation for the rating range.

findings.title: Missing Content-Security-Policy Header
findings.description: The application does not set a Content-Security-Policy (CSP) header on any response. This absence directly enables the confirmed DOM XSS vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary JavaScript without any browser-side mitigation. A properly configured CSP with script-src restrictions could prevent inline script execution and mitigate XSS attacks even when injection points exist. The lack of CSP combined with the confirmed DOM XSS creates a high-risk attack chain for session hijacking and data theft.

findings.title: Application Configuration Exposed Without Authentication
findings.description: The endpoint /rest/admin/application-configuration returns the complete application configuration (23,448 bytes) without requiring authentication. This includes server configuration (port, base URL), application domain, chatbot model configuration (model name: gemma4:e4b), social media URLs, product catalog with pricing details, user review authors (revealing usernames: admin, bender, jim, morty, etc.), and other internal application settings. While labeled as an 'admin' endpoint, it is accessible to unauthenticated users, leaking internal application architecture details that can aid further attacks.

findings.title: Forged Feedback via UserId Mass Assignment
findings.description: The /api/Feedbacks/ POST endpoint accepts a UserId parameter in the request body, allowing an authenticated user to create feedback entries attributed to any other user. By submitting {"UserId": 2} in the feedback request body while authenticated as admin (user ID 1), the feedback was created with UserId=2, effectively impersonating another user's feedback. This is a mass assignment vulnerability where the server does not filter user-controllable fields that should be server-side determined.

findings.title: Privilege Escalation via Mass Assignment on User Registration - Admin Role
findings.description: The user registration endpoint POST /api/Users/ accepts a 'role' parameter in the request body, allowing any unauthenticated user to register a new account with admin privileges. By including {"role": "admin"} in the registration request, a new user was created with role='admin', effectively granting full administrative access without any authentication or authorization. The server assigned profileImage to 'defaultAdmin.png', confirming admin role acceptance. This is a critical mass assignment vulnerability that completely bypasses access controls.

findings.title: Null Byte Injection Bypasses FTP File Extension Filter - Sensitive File Access
findings.description: The /ftp/ directory listing restricts access to certain file extensions (.bak, .gg), returning HTTP 403. However, appending %2500.md (double-encoded null byte followed by an allowed extension) bypasses the extension filter. This was exploited to access: (1) package.json.bak containing the application's npm dependencies and version (juice-shop 6.2.0-SNAPSHOT), (2) coupons_2013.md.bak containing encoded coupon codes, and (3) eastere.gg containing the application's easter egg text. The null byte terminates the filename at the OS level while the web server validates the appended .md extension.

findings.title: Password Change via GET Request - CSRF Exploitable
findings.description: The password change functionality at /rest/user/change-password accepts GET requests with the current and new passwords as query parameters. Combined with the complete absence of CSRF tokens in the application, this allows an attacker to change any authenticated user's password by tricking them into visiting a crafted URL. The password was successfully changed via GET /rest/user/change-password?current=admin123&new=newpassword&repeat=newpassword, returning HTTP 200 with a new password hash (5e9d11a14ad1c8dd77e98ef9b53fd1ba). No CSRF tokens, no SameSite=Strict cookies, and no re-authentication required.

findings.title: Password Change Response Leaks Password Hash
findings.description: The password change endpoint at /rest/user/change-password returns the full user object in its response, including the MD5 password hash of the newly set password. After changing the admin password, the response body contained the new hash 5e9d11a14ad1c8dd77e98ef9b53fd1ba. This information disclosure enables an attacker who has compromised a session to immediately obtain the password hash for offline cracking, even if they don't know the original password that was set. The hash uses unsalted MD5, which is trivially reversible.

findings.title: DOM XSS to Session Hijacking - Full Cookie and Token Theft Chain
findings.description: The confirmed DOM XSS vulnerability in the search functionality was weaponized into a complete session hijacking attack chain. A crafted URL with the payload <img src=x onerror="window.__stolen=document.cookie"> successfully exfiltrated the full authentication token from both document.cookie and localStorage. The stolen JWT token was then reused in a separate browser context to access admin APIs (HTTP 200), confirming full account takeover. No CSP, non-httpOnly cookies, and JWT in localStorage create a perfect storm for session theft via XSS.

findings.title: Prometheus Metrics Endpoint Exposed Without Authentication
findings.description: The /metrics endpoint exposes Prometheus metrics (26,051 bytes) without authentication. This reveals operational data including: HTTP request counts by status code (957 2XX, 18 5XX, 33 4XX, 208 3XX), CPU usage (26.8s user time), challenge completion status (juiceshop_challenges_solved by difficulty and category), and process-level metrics. While this doesn't directly expose user data, it reveals application internals, error rates, and security challenge status that could aid an attacker in understanding the application's state and planning further attacks.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS on All API Endpoints Including Sensitive Data
findings.description: All API endpoints return Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * header, including sensitive endpoints like /api/Users (user listing), /api/Products, and /rest/admin/application-configuration. While the wildcard CORS does not allow credentials (browsers refuse to send credentials with wildcard origin), it enables any website to read API responses for unauthenticated endpoints. Since the admin configuration, product catalog, security questions, and challenge data are accessible without authentication, any third-party website can silently read this data via cross-origin requests.

findings.title: Negative Quantity Accepted in Basket Items - Business Logic Bypass
findings.description: The /api/BasketItems/{id} PUT endpoint accepts negative quantity values without server-side validation. By sending {"quantity": -5} to update a basket item, the server accepted the change (HTTP 200) and stored the negative quantity. This could be exploited to manipulate order totals, potentially resulting in negative prices or credits at checkout. The original quantity was 2 and was changed to -5, with the server responding with a success status.

findings.title: JWT Algorithm None Attack - Authentication Bypass
findings.mitreAttackName: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token
findings.description: The application accepts JWT tokens with the algorithm set to 'none', completely bypassing signature verification. By crafting a JWT with header {"typ":"JWT","alg":"none"} and any desired payload (including admin role and arbitrary user ID), the token is accepted by the server without any signature. This was confirmed by sending a crafted alg:none token to /rest/user/whoami which returned the admin user data (HTTP 200). An attacker can impersonate any user by simply base64-encoding a forged JWT payload with no signature.

findings.title: Security Questions Exposed Without Authentication
findings.description: The /rest/user/security-question endpoint allows unauthenticated users to retrieve the security question assigned to any email address. By providing email=admin@juice-sh.op, the response reveals that the admin's security question is 'Mother's maiden name?' (question ID 2). This information aids in password reset attacks by revealing which question to research/social engineer, and confirms that a given email address exists in the system (user enumeration).

findings.title: JWT Public Key Exposed at /encryptionkeys/jwt.pub
findings.description: The RSA public key used for JWT signature verification is exposed at /encryptionkeys/jwt.pub without authentication. While the public key alone doesn't compromise authentication, it enables RS256-to-HS256 algorithm confusion attacks where an attacker could craft valid JWTs signed with the public key as an HMAC secret. The key format is RSA (MIGJAoGBAM3CosR73CBN...) and the JWT uses RS256 signing. Combined with the confirmed alg:none bypass, this further weakens the JWT security posture.
